questions.q: Which statement best defines biodiversity?
options: The variety of life from genes to ecosystems
The total count of individual animals living in a forest
The scientific study of how organisms interact with climate
The number of protected areas legally notified in a country
questions.explain: Biodiversity is the total variety of living organisms and the ecosystems they form, including the genetic variation within species.
why_wrong: That is population size, not variety of life.
That describes ecology, not the variety of life itself.
Protected areas are a conservation tool, not the definition.

questions.q: Variation of genes within a single species is called
questions.explain: Genetic diversity is the variation in genes among individuals and populations of one species, such as the many varieties of rice.
why_wrong: Species diversity is the variety of different species, not genes within one species.
Ecosystem diversity is the variety of habitats and ecosystems.
This is not a recognised level of biodiversity.

questions.q: The variety of different species in a region is known as
questions.explain: Species diversity covers how many different species live in a region and how evenly they are represented.
why_wrong: Genetic diversity is variation within a species.
Ecosystem diversity is variety of habitat types, not species.
Cultural diversity concerns human societies, not species.

questions.q: Forests, grasslands, wetlands and deserts occurring in one country illustrate which level of biodiversity?
questions.explain: Ecosystem diversity refers to the variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in an area.
why_wrong: Genetic diversity refers to gene variation within a species.
Species diversity counts different species, not habitat types.
This is not one of the three standard levels.

questions.q: The term 'biodiversity' was popularised by which scientist?
questions.explain: E. O. Wilson popularised the word after the 1986 National Forum on BioDiversity and his 1988 book of the same name.
why_wrong: Darwin proposed natural selection and did not use the word biodiversity.
Carson wrote Silent Spring about pesticides.
Myers proposed the hotspot concept, not the term biodiversity.

questions.q: Species diversity generally reaches its highest value in which region of the world?
questions.explain: Warm, stable and productive tropical climates have supported more species than temperate or polar regions.
why_wrong: Polar regions have very few species due to extreme cold.
These have moderate diversity, lower than the tropics.
Deserts have low diversity because water is scarce.

questions.q: Pollination of crops by bees is an example of a(n)
questions.explain: Pollinators provide a service that supports crop production and natural plant reproduction without human payment.
why_wrong: Pollination benefits ecosystems and people, it is not a hazard.
Invasion refers to alien species spreading, not pollination.
A bottleneck is a sharp drop in population variation.

questions.q: Food, fuelwood, fibre and fresh water supplied by ecosystems are called
questions.explain: Provisioning services are the products people obtain directly from ecosystems.
why_wrong: Regulating services control processes like climate, floods and disease.
Cultural services are non-material benefits such as recreation.
Supporting services such as nutrient cycling underpin all other services.

questions.q: The enjoyment people get from the beauty of forests, flowers and wildlife reflects which value of biodiversity?
questions.explain: Aesthetic value is the appreciation of natural beauty, which also drives nature tourism.
why_wrong: Consumptive value involves using resources directly, such as fuelwood.
Productive value comes from marketed products.
Option value is the potential future use of a resource.

questions.q: Using biodiversity for scientific research, education and monitoring of environmental change is its
questions.explain: Species and ecosystems are sources of knowledge for science, teaching and bioindication.
why_wrong: Consumptive value means local direct use for subsistence.
Aesthetic value relates to beauty and enjoyment.
Commercial value relates to trade, not knowledge.

questions.q: Which of the following is a direct economic benefit of forest biodiversity?
questions.explain: Timber, medicines, resins and fruits are harvested and sold, giving direct economic value.
why_wrong: This is an indirect regulating benefit.
This is an indirect ecological benefit.
This is an aesthetic value, not a harvested product.

questions.q: Nutrient cycling and soil formation are examples of which value or service of biodiversity?
questions.explain: They maintain the basic processes on which ecosystems and all other services depend.
why_wrong: Aesthetic value concerns beauty, not ecosystem processes.
Recreation is a cultural benefit.
These processes are not directly traded in markets.

questions.q: Who introduced the concept of biodiversity hotspots in 1988?
questions.explain: Norman Myers identified regions rich in endemic species and under severe threat.
why_wrong: Wilson popularised the term biodiversity.
Elton is known for food webs and ecological niche work.
Whittaker defined alpha, beta and gamma diversity.

questions.q: A biodiversity hotspot is an area that has
options: no human presence or settlement at all
only marine species and coral reefs
questions.explain: A hotspot holds many endemic species and has lost most of its original habitat.
why_wrong: Hotspots are defined by rare, endemic species.
Many hotspots are densely populated and threatened by people.
Hotspots include land regions as well.

questions.q: Which of the following is a biodiversity hotspot in India?
questions.explain: The Western Ghats, with Sri Lanka, form a recognised global hotspot.
why_wrong: The Thar is an arid zone, not a recognised hotspot.
The plain is largely cultivated and is not a hotspot.
This is not a recognised hotspot.

questions.q: Species found only in a particular geographic area and nowhere else are called
questions.explain: Endemism is the restriction of a species to a defined region.
why_wrong: Exotic species are introduced from other regions.
Cosmopolitan species occur widely across the world.
Keystone species have a large ecological effect, regardless of range.

questions.q: To qualify as a hotspot, a region must have lost at least what portion of its original habitat?
questions.explain: Along with 1,500 endemic plant species, a hotspot must have lost at least 70 percent of its primary vegetation.
why_wrong: Too low for a hotspot threshold.
Too low for a hotspot threshold.
This is below the accepted 70 percent threshold.

questions.q: Which organisation is best known for identifying and updating the global list of hotspots?
questions.explain: It adopted and refined Myers' hotspot concept and maintains the list.
why_wrong: The WTO deals with trade rules.
The IMF deals with finance.
The FAO focuses on agriculture and food, not the hotspot list.

questions.q: What is generally considered the greatest threat to biodiversity worldwide?
questions.explain: Clearing, fragmentation and degradation of habitats affect more species than any other pressure.
why_wrong: These are local events with minor global effect.
Not a significant cause of biodiversity loss.
A normal climate pattern, not a threat.

questions.q: Illegal hunting and trading of wild animals is called
questions.explain: Poaching is the unlawful killing or capturing of wildlife.
why_wrong: Grazing means animals feeding on vegetation.
Afforestation is planting trees.
Bioprospecting is searching for useful biological material.

questions.q: A species that is introduced into a new area and spreads harmfully there is known as
questions.explain: Such species lack natural enemies and outcompete native ones.
why_wrong: Endemics are native and restricted to their region.
Keystone species are important in their own native ecosystems.
Flagship species are used to attract public conservation support.

questions.q: Which aquatic plant, called the 'Terror of Bengal', is a notorious invasive species in India?
questions.explain: Eichhornia crassipes chokes water bodies and depletes oxygen.
why_wrong: Lotus is native and not considered an invasive threat.
Not the plant given this nickname.
Mangrove forests are native coastal vegetation.

questions.q: Conflict between people and wild animals over space and resources is called
questions.explain: It occurs when wildlife damages crops, livestock or lives, and people retaliate.
why_wrong: Commensalism is an ecological interaction where one benefits and the other is unaffected.
Symbiosis is a mutually beneficial interaction.
Biomagnification is the build-up of toxins up the food chain.

questions.q: Breaking of a large continuous habitat into small isolated patches is known as
questions.explain: Roads, farmland and dams often split habitats and isolate populations.
why_wrong: Restoration means repairing damaged habitats.
Succession is the natural change in community structure over time.
Enrichment means improving habitat quality.

questions.q: The fine shahtoosh wool, whose trade drives poaching, comes from which animal?
questions.explain: Chiru are killed for their under-fur, which is illegal to trade.
why_wrong: Pashmina is shorn from domestic goats and is legal.
Yaks are domesticated for milk and hair.
Merino wool is from domestic sheep.

questions.q: Ivory, a major target of poachers, is obtained from the tusks of
questions.explain: Ivory trade has caused severe population declines in elephants.
why_wrong: Rhinos are poached for their horn, not ivory.
Musk deer are killed for the musk gland.
Leopards are hunted for skin and claws.

questions.q: A species of which no living individual remains anywhere is called
questions.explain: Extinct means the last individual has died.
why_wrong: Endangered species still have living members but are at high risk.
Vulnerable species still survive in the wild.
Rare species still exist.

questions.q: Which of these birds is a well-known extinct species?
questions.explain: The dodo of Mauritius was driven extinct in the 1600s by hunting and introduced animals.
why_wrong: Still survives, though critically endangered.
Common and widespread.
Still survives in India.

questions.q: A species facing a very high risk of extinction in the near future is classified as
questions.explain: Endangered species are in danger of extinction if factors causing decline continue.
why_wrong: No living individuals remain in that case.
Least concern species are not at significant risk.
Vulnerable species face a lower risk than endangered ones.

questions.q: Species likely to become endangered if present threats continue are called
questions.explain: Vulnerable species are facing high risk of extinction in the wild in the medium term.
why_wrong: Extinct species have no survivors.
Common species are abundant.
Exotic means introduced from elsewhere.

questions.q: Species with small populations that are not yet endangered or vulnerable but are at risk are called
questions.explain: Rare species are localised or thinly spread and could become threatened.
why_wrong: No living individuals remain.
Keystone refers to ecological importance, not population size.
Pests are species harmful to human interests.

questions.q: EDGE species stands for
options: Ecologically Diverse and Geographically Established species
Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered species
questions.explain: These are threatened species with few close relatives, so their loss removes unique evolutionary history.
why_wrong: This expansion is invented.
Not the meaning of EDGE.
Not the meaning of EDGE.

questions.q: Conserving species in their natural habitat is called
questions.explain: In-situ means 'on site'; the species is protected where it lives.
why_wrong: Ex-situ means off-site conservation.
Bioprospecting is the search for valuable biological products.
Biomagnification is toxin accumulation in food chains.

questions.q: Conservation of species outside their natural habitat is known as
questions.explain: Ex-situ means 'off site', as in zoos and gene banks.
why_wrong: In-situ is conservation within the natural habitat.
Not the term used for habitat-based conservation types.
This is in-situ conservation.

questions.q: Which of the following is an in-situ conservation measure?
questions.explain: National parks protect wildlife and habitats where they naturally occur.
why_wrong: A zoo is an ex-situ facility.
Seed banks store germplasm outside natural habitats.
Botanical gardens are ex-situ.

questions.q: Which of the following is an ex-situ conservation facility?
questions.explain: Plants are grown outside their natural habitat for conservation and study.
why_wrong: Sanctuaries protect wildlife in their natural habitat.
Biosphere reserves are in-situ.
Sacred groves protect species where they naturally occur.

questions.q: Storing seeds, sperm or tissues at very low temperature for long-term preservation is part of
questions.explain: Gene banks preserve genetic resources outside the habitat.
why_wrong: Corridors link habitats on the ground.
A park conserves species in situ.
Sacred groves are in-situ, community protected.

questions.q: Project Tiger, India's flagship conservation programme for tigers, was launched in
questions.explain: It was started in 1973 with a set of tiger reserves.
why_wrong: This was India's independence year.
Not the year of Project Tiger.
Not the year of Project Tiger.

questions.q: Patches of forest protected by local communities on religious grounds are called
questions.explain: They are traditional in-situ conservation sites in many parts of India.
why_wrong: These are managed ex-situ collections.
These are managed for hunting, not religious protection.
These store seeds artificially.

questions.q: In a biosphere reserve, the innermost, strictly protected area is the
questions.explain: The core zone holds undisturbed ecosystems with minimum human activity.
why_wrong: The buffer surrounds the core and allows limited activities.
The transition zone is the outermost area with human settlement.
Not an official zone of the biosphere reserve model.

questions.q: How many biogeographic zones are recognised in India?
questions.explain: India has ten zones, including Trans-Himalaya, Desert and Islands.
why_wrong: Too few for the classification.
Too few for the classification.
Too many for the classification.

questions.q: India is regarded as a
questions.explain: India is one of the roughly seventeen countries holding most of the world's biodiversity.
why_wrong: This is not a real category.
India's species wealth is among the highest.
India contains several global hotspots.

questions.q: Which is the largest of India's biogeographic zones?
questions.explain: It covers a very large part of peninsular India.
why_wrong: This is a high, cold zone with a smaller area.
Islands cover a small area.
Coasts form a narrow belt.

questions.q: The Thar and Kutch region belongs to which biogeographic zone?
questions.explain: It includes arid and semi-arid regions of Rajasthan and Kutch.
why_wrong: This lies in the fertile plain of north India.
This is a humid hill range in the west.
This is a high-rainfall hill region.

questions.q: The Andaman and Nicobar group and Lakshadweep belong to which biogeographic zone?
questions.explain: These island groups form the Islands zone of India.
why_wrong: The Coasts zone covers mainland coastline.
Not related to islands.
This is a high mountain cold desert zone.

questions.q: The existence of hundreds of mango varieties in India best illustrates
questions.explain: The varieties belong to one species, so the variation is within-species gene variation.
why_wrong: That would need many different species.
That would involve different habitats.
This is not a standard level.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three recognised levels of biodiversity?
questions.explain: The three standard levels are genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
why_wrong: It is a recognised level.
It is a recognised level.
It is a recognised level.

questions.q: In Whittaker's scheme, beta diversity measures
options: the count of species within one habitat
the total species in an entire region
the gene variation within one species
questions.explain: Beta diversity compares how different the species sets are between habitats along a gradient.
why_wrong: This is alpha diversity.
This is gamma diversity.
This is genetic diversity, not beta diversity.

questions.q: Species richness refers to
options: the number of different species in an area
how evenly individuals are spread among species
the number of ecosystems in a region
questions.explain: It is a simple count of species, ignoring how many individuals each has.
why_wrong: That is species evenness.
That is abundance.
That is ecosystem diversity.

questions.q: Which of the following explains why tropical regions hold more species than polar ones?
options: Fewer predators and parasites in the tropics
Warm stable climate over long time
A much smaller total land area
questions.explain: Constant warmth and high productivity allowed species to accumulate and persist.
why_wrong: This is not a general explanation.
Tropical areas generally have high rainfall.
The tropics are very large.

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a level of diversity with an example?
options: Genetic diversity - forests, deserts and wetlands together
Species diversity - many species in a rainforest
Ecosystem diversity - many varieties of one crop
Genetic diversity - number of national parks in India
questions.explain: Species diversity describes the variety of species living together.
why_wrong: That example is ecosystem diversity.
That example is genetic diversity.
Not an example of genes within a species.

questions.q: Wetlands absorbing floodwater and reducing flood damage is an example of a
questions.explain: Regulating services moderate natural processes such as floods, climate and water quality.
why_wrong: Provisioning gives products such as food and water.
Cultural benefits are recreational or spiritual.
Supporting services cover basic processes like soil formation.

questions.q: Which of the following is a supporting ecosystem service?
questions.explain: Supporting services underlie all other services.
why_wrong: This is a provisioning service.
This is a cultural service.
This is a regulating service.

questions.q: Pilgrimage to sacred rivers and recreation in national parks are examples of
questions.explain: These are non-material benefits such as spiritual and recreational value.
why_wrong: They do not supply material products.
They do not regulate natural processes.
They are not basic ecosystem processes.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit that ecosystems provide to people?
questions.explain: Ozone depletion is a harm caused by human pollutants.
why_wrong: It is a regulating benefit.
It is a regulating and supporting benefit.
It is a provisioning benefit.

questions.q: The anticancer drug vincristine obtained from the rosy periwinkle illustrates the
options: aesthetic value of biodiversity and beauty
ethical value of all living species
regulating value of climate and water
questions.explain: Species can supply drugs of great economic value, so loss of species means losing potential medicines.
why_wrong: Aesthetic value concerns beauty.
Ethical value says all species have a right to exist.
Not related to drug production.

questions.q: The view that all species have an inherent right to exist, regardless of their usefulness to humans, is the
options: consumptive value of local direct use
option value of future potential benefits
questions.explain: It treats species as valuable in themselves.
why_wrong: Commercial value depends on market use.
Consumptive value is about direct use.
Option value is about future possible benefits.

questions.q: Protection of sacred groves by villagers mainly demonstrates which value?
questions.explain: The groves are protected because of community beliefs and traditions.
why_wrong: They are not protected for trade.
They are not protected for industry.
They have no defence role.

questions.q: Which pair contains hotspots that lie wholly or partly in India?
options: California Floristic Province and Mediterranean Basin
questions.explain: Both regions extend into India, along with the Western Ghats and Sundaland (Nicobar).
why_wrong: Neither lies in India.
Neither lies in India.
Neither lies in India.

questions.q: Besides habitat loss of at least 70 percent, a region must contain at least how many endemic vascular plant species to qualify as a hotspot?
questions.explain: This is the plant endemism threshold, roughly 0.5 percent of global plant species.
why_wrong: Far too low for the criterion.
Far too high for the criterion.
Not the accepted threshold.

questions.q: Conservation efforts focus on hotspots because
options: they have almost no human population living there
they contain only commercially useful species and crops
they hold many endemic species in little area
they are completely free from any serious threat
questions.explain: Protecting a small area can save a large number of otherwise irreplaceable species.
why_wrong: Many hotspots are densely populated.
The selection is based on endemism and threat.
Being threatened is a defining criterion.

questions.q: The Western Ghats hotspot is combined with which neighbouring country's land?
questions.explain: The hotspot is known as the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka.
why_wrong: Not part of that hotspot.
Not part of that hotspot.
Not part of that hotspot.

questions.q: An exotic species differs from an endemic species in that an exotic species
options: is found nowhere else on earth at all
is always extinct in its original homeland
is always harmless to native species
is introduced from outside the area
questions.explain: Exotics originate elsewhere, whereas endemics are native and restricted to the area.
why_wrong: That describes an endemic species.
Not a definition of exotic species.
Exotics can be invasive and harmful.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a criterion for a region to be called a hotspot?
questions.explain: Parks are management tools and not part of the hotspot criteria.
why_wrong: This is a hotspot criterion.
This is a hotspot criterion.
This is a hotspot criterion.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of habitat loss?
questions.explain: Protected areas shield habitat from loss.
why_wrong: Roads destroy and fragment habitat.
Drainage destroys wetland habitat.
Mining removes habitat.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an invasive alien species in India?
questions.explain: Sal is a native forest tree of India.
why_wrong: Introduced ornamental that spreads in forests.
Introduced weed that spreads in fields and wastelands.
Introduced aquatic weed.

questions.q: The introduction of Nile perch into Lake Victoria is a classic example of
options: successful biological conservation of native fish
native fish loss due to an invasive predator
natural migration of fish into the lake
genetic enrichment of native cichlid fish
questions.explain: Nile perch preyed on and competed with native cichlids, causing many to disappear.
why_wrong: It harmed native biodiversity.
The fish was deliberately introduced.
It caused losses of cichlids rather than enrichment.

questions.q: Invasive alien species spread rapidly in new areas mainly because
options: they cannot reproduce quickly in new areas
native species protect them from harm
they need very specific narrow habitats
they have no natural enemies there
questions.explain: Without checks from their home ecosystem, populations expand and displace natives.
why_wrong: Rapid reproduction aids invasion.
Native species usually compete with them.
Invaders are usually tolerant generalists.

questions.q: Elephants raiding crops in villages near forests is most directly linked to
options: too much forest area left for them
a lack of crops in the whole region
questions.explain: Fragmentation pushes elephants into farmland in search of food.
why_wrong: Habitat is shrinking rather than expanding.
Crops attract elephants when forests lack food.
Conflict occurs where people and elephants overlap.

questions.q: Which animal is persistently poached for its horn?
questions.explain: Its horn is illegally traded, so Kaziranga guards it heavily.
why_wrong: Elephants are poached for ivory.
Tigers are poached for skin and bones.
Poached for pelts and bones.

questions.q: Poaching differs from legal wildlife use mainly because it is
options: done only at night by trained hunters
done only for food by hungry villagers
done only by local tribal communities
questions.explain: Poaching violates law, such as the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
why_wrong: Timing does not define poaching.
Many poachers target trophies or trade, not food.
Poachers can be anyone.

questions.q: Which measure helps reduce human-wildlife conflict?
options: Removing all forests near every village
Encouraging encroachment into reserves and forests
questions.explain: Corridors give animals safe passage and early warnings keep people safe.
why_wrong: This increases habitat loss and worsens conflict.
This makes animals depend on people and increases conflict.
This increases overlap and conflict.

questions.q: In the Sundarbans, human-tiger conflict is highest for people who
options: enter the mangroves to fish or collect honey
live in distant big cities far away
work in offices in nearby towns
stay on boats in the open sea only
questions.explain: They work inside tiger territory, so attacks occur.
why_wrong: They are not exposed to tigers.
They have no tiger encounters.
The risk is mainly for those entering the forest.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly lists IUCN threat categories from higher to lower risk?
options: Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Near Threatened
Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered
Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened
Endangered, Critically Endangered, Near Threatened, Vulnerable
questions.explain: Critically endangered species face the highest risk, followed by endangered and vulnerable.
why_wrong: This reverses the correct order.
This is the exact reverse.
Mixed up order.

questions.q: Which large cat was declared extinct in India in 1952?
questions.explain: The Asiatic cheetah vanished in India due to hunting and habitat loss.
why_wrong: Still survives in Gir.
Survives in high Himalayan areas.
Survives in north-eastern India.

questions.q: A species surviving only in captivity or cultivation is classed as
questions.explain: It no longer lives naturally in the wild but still has captive individuals.
why_wrong: Extinct means no living individuals anywhere.
Vulnerable species still live in the wild.
This means insufficient information, not captivity.

questions.q: Why are EDGE species given special conservation priority?
options: They are common and widespread across many regions
They are all large mammals found in forests
They are threatened and have few close relatives
They are all invasive species of wetlands
questions.explain: The unique evolutionary history of such species cannot be replaced by relatives.
why_wrong: Common species are not a conservation priority.
EDGE includes birds, reptiles, amphibians and others.
They are native and threatened.

questions.q: The IUCN Red Data Book is best described as
options: a list of species and threat status
a catalogue of all national parks
a guide to managing zoo animals
a list of common species only
questions.explain: It documents the conservation status of species.
why_wrong: Parks are listed elsewhere.
Not its purpose.
It concerns threatened species.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an extinct species?
questions.explain: The snow leopard survives in the Himalayas.
why_wrong: It is extinct.
It is extinct since 1914.
It is extinct, the last known one died in 1936.

questions.q: The main difference between endangered and vulnerable species is that
options: vulnerable species are already extinct today
endangered species face a higher extinction risk
endangered species are always invasive aliens
vulnerable species live only inside zoos
questions.explain: Vulnerable species face a lower, medium-term risk.
why_wrong: Extinct species are a separate category.
Invasiveness is unrelated to threat status.
Vulnerable species live in the wild.

questions.q: How does a national park differ from a wildlife sanctuary?
options: A national park bans human activities like grazing
A national park allows regulated hunting inside
A sanctuary is an ex-situ site like a zoo
A national park is always smaller in area
questions.explain: Sanctuaries may allow some activities while national parks are strictly protected.
why_wrong: Hunting is prohibited in national parks.
Sanctuaries are in-situ sites.
Size is not the distinguishing factor.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an ex-situ conservation method?
questions.explain: Biosphere reserves protect ecosystems in their natural place.
why_wrong: A zoo is ex-situ.
This is ex-situ.
This is ex-situ.

questions.q: Preserving sperm, embryos or plant tissue in liquid nitrogen is called
questions.explain: Very low temperature stops biological activity, so material can be stored for years.
why_wrong: A heat treatment for milk.
Cold treatment to induce flowering.
Using organisms to clean up pollution.

questions.q: Which national park is the protected home of the Asiatic lion?
questions.explain: Gir in Gujarat is the last natural habitat of the Asiatic lion.
why_wrong: Known for the one-horned rhino.
Known for water birds.
Known for tigers and was India's first national park.

questions.q: Captive breeding followed by reintroduction into the wild is a strategy of
questions.explain: Individuals are bred outside and released to rebuild wild populations.
why_wrong: Captive breeding takes place outside the natural habitat.
Not designed for pests.
Not designed for commercial farming.

questions.q: The correct order of zones in a biosphere reserve from the centre outward is
questions.explain: The core is strictly protected, the buffer allows compatible activity, and the transition area allows settlement.
why_wrong: The core lies at the centre.
This reverses the order.
The buffer lies between core and transition.

questions.q: A key advantage of in-situ over ex-situ conservation is that in-situ conservation
options: can be carried out only inside zoos and parks
needs no land set aside or legal protection
guarantees complete freedom from all threats
keeps species evolving within their natural habitat
questions.explain: Species remain within their ecosystem interactions and adaptive processes.
why_wrong: Zoos are ex-situ.
It requires protected land.
Threats can still occur in protected areas.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a seed bank from a botanical garden?
options: A seed bank is in-situ while a botanical garden is ex-situ
A seed bank stores seeds cold; a garden grows live plants
A seed bank grows whole trees inside natural forests
A botanical garden stores only animal tissue samples
questions.explain: Both are ex-situ methods but differ in how plants are maintained.
why_wrong: Both are ex-situ.
Seed banks store seeds, not forests.
They hold plants, not animal tissue.

questions.q: Which biogeographic zone includes the Malabar coast hill forests of Kerala and Karnataka?
questions.explain: The zone is a rainy chain of hills along the west coast.
why_wrong: A cold arid high-altitude zone.
A fertile alluvial plain in the north.
A dry zone from Punjab through Gujarat.

questions.q: India qualifies as a mega-diversity nation chiefly because it
options: has the largest land area of any country in the world
contains no endangered species at all anywhere
holds many species, endemics and several hotspots
has only tropical rainforests across its whole area
questions.explain: Its varied climates and landscapes support rich life and many endemics.
why_wrong: India is not the world's largest country.
India has many threatened species.
India has deserts, mountains, wetlands and many other ecosystems.

questions.q: A botanist in Uttar Pradesh catalogues 30 distinct varieties of mango, all belonging to Mangifera indica, each differing in taste, size and ripening time. Which level of biodiversity does this variation represent?
questions.explain: Variation among individuals and varieties within a single species is genetic diversity, and the mango varieties are all one species.
why_wrong: All the varieties belong to one species, so the number of species is unchanged.
No variety of habitats or ecosystems is being compared here.
Beta diversity measures change in species composition between habitats, not variation inside one species.

questions.q: Two forest patches each contain 4 tree species. In patch A each species has 100 individuals; in patch B one species has 385 individuals and the other three have 5 each. Which statement is correct?
options: Patch B has higher species richness because one species dominates
Patch A has higher richness because it has more individuals
Both have equal species richness, but patch A has greater evenness
Both patches have identical species diversity in every sense
questions.explain: Richness counts species only, so both equal 4; species diversity also considers relative abundance, and patch A is far more even.
why_wrong: Dominance by one species does not raise richness; richness is just the species count.
Richness does not depend on the number of individuals.
Their relative abundances differ, so evenness and overall diversity differ.

questions.q: While surveying a coastal state, a student compares a mangrove swamp, a coral reef, a sand-dune scrub and an inland grassland. The variety she is recording is best called
questions.explain: Variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in a region is ecosystem diversity.
why_wrong: She is not comparing gene variation within a species.
Richness counts species, whereas she is comparing different habitat types.
Alpha diversity is species diversity within one habitat, not across habitat types.

questions.q: Walking up a Himalayan slope from the foothills to the alpine meadows, a trekker notices the set of species changes sharply every few hundred metres. This turnover of species between habitats along the gradient is
questions.explain: Beta diversity measures the change in species composition from one habitat to another along a gradient.
why_wrong: Alpha diversity is the species diversity within a single habitat, not change between habitats.
Gamma diversity is the total diversity of a whole landscape or region.
This concerns species composition, not variation inside a species.

questions.q: A large, continuous population of an Indian tiger subspecies is reduced to a few isolated groups. Species count in the region is unchanged, yet inbreeding depression appears. Which level of biodiversity has declined?
questions.explain: Isolation and small population size reduce heterozygosity and cause inbreeding, which is loss of genetic diversity even though species richness is unchanged.
why_wrong: The number of species in the region has not changed.
The ecosystems themselves are intact; only variation within the species is lost.
Gamma diversity is regional species diversity, which is unchanged here.

questions.q: The Green Revolution replaced thousands of traditional rice landraces with a handful of high-yielding varieties across Indian fields. This loss of allelic variety is called
questions.explain: Genetic erosion is the loss of genetic variation in a crop or species, here from replacing many landraces with few uniform varieties.
why_wrong: The species Oryza sativa remains; only its varieties were lost.
This describes breaking of habitat, not loss of crop varieties.
Succession is directional change in community structure over time, unrelated to losing varieties.

questions.q: A landscape has many different habitats, each habitat holding only a few species, but almost no species overlap between habitats. Which combination describes it?
options: Low alpha, high beta, high gamma diversity
High alpha, low beta, low gamma diversity
High alpha, high beta, low gamma diversity
Low alpha, low beta, low gamma diversity
questions.explain: Few species per habitat means low alpha, little overlap means high beta, and the many habitats together give high gamma diversity.
why_wrong: Alpha is low here because each habitat has few species.
Alpha is low, and high beta across many habitats makes gamma high, not low.
Little overlap between habitats means beta is high, not low.

questions.q: A student surveys birds along a transect from the cold desert of Ladakh to the Western Ghats of Kerala. Following the general latitudinal gradient, species richness is expected to
options: Be higher in the lower-latitude, tropical end
Be higher in the cold desert end
Be highest midway at the Deccan plateau only
questions.explain: Species richness generally increases from the poles toward the equator, so the tropical southern end is richer.
why_wrong: Harsh cold deserts support fewer species, not more.
The latitudinal gradient predicts a clear increase towards the tropics.
The gradient is not a peak at mid-latitude; tropical regions hold the greatest richness.

questions.q: Under the Convention on Biological Diversity definition, which of the following is NOT itself a component of biological diversity?
questions.explain: The CBD covers diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems; abiotic climate variation is not biodiversity itself.
why_wrong: This is genetic diversity, explicitly part of the definition.
This is species diversity, explicitly part of the definition.
This is ecosystem diversity, explicitly part of the definition.

questions.q: A city wetland absorbs monsoon floodwater and filters pollutants, while nearby villagers also catch fish from it. Which pair correctly classifies these benefits?
options: Flood control is a regulating service; fish catch is a provisioning service
Flood control is a provisioning service; fish catch is a cultural service
Flood control is a cultural service; fish catch is a regulating service
questions.explain: Regulating services moderate natural processes like floods, while provisioning services supply products like food.
why_wrong: Flood control is regulation, and fish are a material product, not a cultural benefit.
Neither benefit is cultural or regulating in that way.
Supporting services are basic processes like nutrient cycling, not these end benefits.

questions.q: A pharmaceutical firm screens rainforest plants and fungi for chemical compounds that could become new drugs. The value of biodiversity being exploited is mainly its
questions.explain: Genetic and chemical information in organisms, used in bioprospecting and research, is informational value.
why_wrong: The firm is not valuing beauty or recreation.
Existence value is worth placed on a species merely existing, without use.
Nobody is visiting for leisure here.

questions.q: Villagers in the Western Ghats refuse to cut a grove of ancient trees, even though the timber is valuable, because it is dedicated to a local deity. This reflects the
questions.explain: Spiritual and cultural attachment to nature, such as sacred groves, is a social value of biodiversity.
why_wrong: Consumptive use means harvesting resources, which villagers are refusing to do.
Productive use involves selling harvested goods, which is not the motive.
They are not valuing the grove for research or genetic information.

questions.q: After pesticide spraying kills most wild bees near an orchard, fruit set drops sharply. Which ecosystem service has been impaired?
questions.explain: Wild bees pollinate flowers, a regulating service, and fruit set depends directly on it.
why_wrong: Bees play no direct role in purifying water.
Soil formation is a supporting process not driven by bee loss.
Carbon storage is by plant biomass, not by pollinators.

questions.q: A small town earns income from tourists who visit a national park only to watch and photograph wildlife, without removing anything. This is best described as
questions.explain: Benefits gained without harvesting or destroying the resource, like wildlife tourism, are non-consumptive use values.
why_wrong: Nothing is harvested or consumed locally.
Existence value involves no use at all, but tourists are using the park.
Bequest value concerns preservation for future generations, not present income.

questions.q: A multinational patents the wound-healing use of turmeric, long known to Indian households, with no consent or benefit sharing for the knowledge holders. This is an example of
questions.explain: Biopiracy is commercial exploitation or patenting of biological resources or traditional knowledge without consent or fair benefit sharing.
why_wrong: Bioremediation is using organisms to clean pollution.
The scenario involves no consent or benefit sharing.
Biomagnification is the increase of toxins up the food chain.

questions.q: A donor funds protection of a rare Himalayan orchid, hoping its compounds might prove medically useful someday, even though no use is known today. This is
questions.explain: Option value is the worth of keeping a resource available for possible future use.
why_wrong: Existence value has no expectation of any use.
Bequest value is about passing the resource to future generations, not a specific hoped-for use.
No present harvesting is involved.

questions.q: Under the four-way ecosystem service classification, nutrient cycling in a forest soil belongs to which category?
questions.explain: Supporting services, such as nutrient cycling and primary production, underpin all other services.
why_wrong: Provisioning services are tangible products like food and timber.
Regulating services moderate climate, floods and disease, not underlying processes.
Cultural services are non-material benefits like recreation and spirituality.

questions.q: Villagers of the Sundarbans collect honey from mangroves, while the same mangroves blunt cyclone surges and local people also revere Bonbibi. Which of these is the PROVISIONING service?
questions.explain: Honey is a material product obtained from the ecosystem, which is a provisioning service.
why_wrong: This is a regulating service.
This is a cultural service.
This is a supporting service.

questions.q: Four regions are assessed. Which one qualifies as a biodiversity hot spot?
options: A region with 2500 endemic plant species but only 20% habitat lost
A region with 900 endemic plant species and 85% habitat lost
A region with 1800 endemic plants and 75% of vegetation lost
A region with 1600 endemic plant species and 40% habitat lost
questions.explain: A hot spot needs at least 1500 endemic vascular plants and at least 70% habitat loss.
why_wrong: It has high endemism but is not sufficiently threatened.
It is threatened but lacks the 1500 endemics required.
Endemism is enough but habitat loss falls short of 70%.

questions.q: A biologist studying the lion-tailed macaque and the Nilgiri tahr is working in which Indian hot spot?
questions.explain: Both are endemic to the Western Ghats, part of the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka hot spot.
why_wrong: These species are not Himalayan.
Indo-Burma covers north-eastern India and Southeast Asia, not these species' range.
Sundaland in India covers only the Nicobar Islands.

questions.q: A survey team is sent to Great Nicobar Island to document endemic plants. Which hot spot does Nicobar belong to?
questions.explain: The Nicobar Islands are the Indian part of the Sundaland hot spot.
why_wrong: Indo-Burma covers the Andaman Islands rather than Nicobar.
This lies on the western side of peninsular India.
This is a mountain hot spot, far from the Nicobar Islands.

questions.q: A conservation trust has funds to protect only a few areas and wants maximum protection of species per rupee. Following the hot spot approach, it should prioritise regions with
options: Large area and low human population
High endemism and severe habitat loss
questions.explain: The hot spot strategy targets places holding many irreplaceable endemic species that are under greatest threat.
why_wrong: Size and low population do not indicate endemism or threat.
Tourism does not indicate biodiversity value.
Such areas hold few irreplaceable species and are already safe.

questions.q: A frog found only in the streams of the Western Ghats and nowhere else on Earth is described as
questions.explain: Endemic species are restricted to one defined geographical area.
why_wrong: Cosmopolitan species occur almost worldwide.
Invasive species are introduced and spread harmfully outside their native range.
Keystone species have outsized effects on their ecosystem, unrelated to range restriction.

questions.q: The Andaman Islands fall within which biodiversity hot spot?
questions.explain: The Andaman group is included in the Indo-Burma hot spot, while the Nicobar group belongs to Sundaland.
why_wrong: Only the Nicobar Islands are in Sundaland.
This hot spot lies on peninsular India's west.
The Himalaya hot spot does not include the Andaman Islands.

questions.q: A report calls Indo-Burma a hot spot, and another calls Brazil a megadiversity country. Which statement correctly links the two terms?
options: Both terms are defined only by national borders
A hot spot must lie entirely within one megadiversity country
A hot spot can cross borders; megadiversity applies to whole countries
Megadiversity depends on habitat loss exceeding 70% of vegetation
questions.explain: Hot spots are defined by biological regions of endemism and threat, whereas megadiversity ranks countries by total diversity.
why_wrong: Hot spots follow biological regions, not borders.
Indo-Burma spans several countries.
The 70% loss criterion is for hot spots, not megadiversity countries.

questions.q: A region has 3000 endemic vascular plant species, but about 60% of its original natural vegetation remains. Why is it not classified as a hot spot?
options: Its endemic plant count exceeds the hot spot limit
Hot spots are defined only by animal endemism
Hot spots cannot contain more than 1500 endemics
It does not meet the threshold of at least 70% habitat loss
questions.explain: Hot spot status requires both high plant endemism and loss of at least 70% of primary vegetation.
why_wrong: There is no upper limit; 3000 easily meets the 1500 minimum.
Hot spot criteria use endemic vascular plants.
No such upper limit exists.

questions.q: A new highway cuts through a continuous forest, splitting a tiger habitat into two small patches. The most likely long-term consequence for the species is
options: Reduced gene flow and higher local extinction risk
Larger home ranges for each tiger
Unaffected population since the total area is the same
questions.explain: Fragmentation isolates populations, causing inbreeding, edge effects and local extinction risk.
why_wrong: Isolation lowers gene flow and diversity.
Smaller patches restrict, not enlarge, ranges.
Fragmentation lowers viable habitat and connectivity even if area is similar.

questions.q: Customs officers seize hundreds of shawls made from the wool of the Tibetan antelope (chiru). The activity behind this seizure is
questions.explain: Chiru are killed for shahtoosh wool, driving poaching for illicit trade.
why_wrong: No introduced species is involved.
The animals are being killed directly, not losing habitat.
This is commercial killing, not clashes over crops or safety.

questions.q: Water hyacinth, native to South America, now chokes lakes and ponds in India, depleting oxygen and killing native fish. Its rapid spread is mainly because it
options: Lacks natural enemies in its new range
Has a very slow reproduction rate
questions.explain: Introduced species often spread fast when predators, pests and competitors from their native range are absent.
why_wrong: It is native to South America.
It floats on water and spreads freely, not soil limited.
It reproduces quickly, which is why it spreads.

questions.q: Wild elephants from a forest fragment in Assam repeatedly raid sugarcane fields at its edge. Which measure best addresses the root cause?
options: Securing forest corridors to reconnect fragments
Capturing and keeping them in zoos
Clearing the remaining forest for more farms
questions.explain: Connecting habitats lets elephants move without entering farms, reducing conflict at its source.
why_wrong: Culling is unlawful for a protected species and does not fix the cause.
Elephants in zoos does not address habitat loss and cannot absorb large herds.
This would worsen habitat loss and conflict.

questions.q: A large dam will submerge a forested river valley that hosts several endemic species. This threat to biodiversity is chiefly
questions.explain: Inundating the valley removes the habitat that the species depend on.
why_wrong: No hunting is involved.
No alien species is introduced.
This is not a recognised biodiversity threat.

questions.q: After forest cover shrinks to small remnants, tigers and other large carnivores vanish before small herbivores do. The best explanation is that large carnivores
options: Are more resistant to edge effects
Depend on a single plant species
Need large ranges and occur at low density
questions.explain: Fragments are too small to sustain viable populations of animals needing big territories.
why_wrong: Large carnivores reproduce slowly.
They are particularly vulnerable to fragmentation.
Their need is space and prey, not one plant.

questions.q: Both African elephants killed for ivory and Indian rhinos killed for horn recover very slowly even after poaching stops. This is mainly because these species
options: Breed several times a year with large litters
Mature late, gestate long and produce few young
questions.explain: Slow life histories give low population growth, so losses are slow to rebuild.
why_wrong: The opposite is true.
They are K-selected, slow to recover.
They need large habitats.

questions.q: Wheat is introduced from abroad and grown across Indian fields but never spreads into forests. Why is it generally NOT considered an invasive alien species?
options: It is a native plant of the Indian subcontinent
It does not form self-sustaining populations harming natives
Invasive species must always be animals, never plants
Every introduced species is automatically invasive everywhere
questions.explain: An introduced species is invasive only if it establishes, spreads and harms native biodiversity or the economy.
why_wrong: Wheat is not native to India.
Plants can be invasive, like Lantana.
Most introduced species never become invasive.

questions.q: Farmers in a village adjoining an Indian forest install beehive fences along their fields to deter elephants. This approach is best described as
options: A cause of forest habitat loss
questions.explain: Elephants avoid bees, so the fence reduces crop raiding without harming the animals.
why_wrong: Animals are not being kept outside their habitat.
Beehive fences do not remove habitat.
Honeybees here are used as a deterrent, not an invading species.

questions.q: A fig wasp depends entirely on one species of fig to breed. If the fig is lost from a forest, the wasp is likely to go extinct. This chain of loss is called
questions.explain: Co-extinction is the loss of a dependent species when its host or partner species disappears.
why_wrong: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency.
This is not the term for dependent loss.
Biomagnification is toxin build-up up the food chain.

questions.q: A district official notes compensation for crop damage by wildlife is paid after years, so villagers poison leopards in retaliation. Which feature of this problem makes it a human-wildlife conflict rather than poaching?
options: Animals are killed for fur in international trade
An alien species has been introduced
The killing is retaliation for losses, not commercial gain
The leopards are kept in captivity
questions.explain: Human-wildlife conflict arises from competition and damage to people, while poaching is killing for trade or profit.
why_wrong: That describes poaching for trade, not retaliation.
No alien species is involved.
The leopards are wild, not captive.

questions.q: A species no longer survives anywhere in the wild, though a few individuals live in a zoo breeding centre. Its IUCN status is
questions.explain: Extinct in the Wild applies when survivors exist only in captivity or cultivation.
why_wrong: Extinct requires that no individual survives anywhere.
This is for wild populations at extreme risk.
This is a lower risk category for living wild populations.

questions.q: A species has a small total population and is not currently endangered or vulnerable, but is at risk because of its restricted range. In the older Red Data Book scheme it is
questions.explain: Rare species have small populations in restricted areas and may quickly become endangered.
why_wrong: The species still survives.
It is not yet at that level of risk.
It is at risk due to restricted range.

questions.q: A crocodilian is the sole surviving member of an ancient family, with no close living relatives, and it is critically endangered worldwide. Conservation planners would flag it as
questions.explain: EDGE means Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered, applying to unique lineages that are also threatened.
why_wrong: Keystone species have a big ecological impact, a different idea.
It is native and threatened, not invasive.
It is far from widespread.

questions.q: A conservationist wants an authoritative document listing threatened species with their risk categories. She should consult
options: The IUCN Red Data Book / Red List
questions.explain: The IUCN Red List documents the extinction-risk status of species.
why_wrong: This lists wetlands of international importance.
This concerns people, not species status.
This lists ozone-depleting substances.

questions.q: A single large carnivore is protected on the expectation that safeguarding its vast forest range will also shelter many other species living there. Such a species is called
questions.explain: Umbrella species have large habitat needs, so protecting them protects many co-occurring species.
why_wrong: It is native, not invasive.
It is still living.
Pioneer species are early colonisers of bare ground.

questions.q: In the EDGE approach, when two species are equally endangered, priority goes to the one with
options: The greater economic value to people
questions.explain: EDGE ranks species by combining evolutionary distinctiveness with threat status.
why_wrong: Size is not a criterion.
Economic value is not part of EDGE.
Range is not the ranking factor.

questions.q: Which sequence lists IUCN categories in increasing order of extinction risk?
options: Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Critically Endangered
Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered
Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Critically Endangered, Endangered
Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened
questions.explain: The risk rises from Near Threatened to Vulnerable to Endangered to Critically Endangered.
why_wrong: Endangered is higher risk than Vulnerable, so the order is wrong.
Near Threatened is lower than Vulnerable, and Endangered precedes Critically Endangered.
This is decreasing order of risk.

questions.q: A newly described frog is known from a single specimen, with no information on its numbers or range. Which IUCN category fits best?
questions.explain: Data Deficient applies when information is inadequate to assess extinction risk.
why_wrong: Least Concern requires evidence of low risk.
Nothing shows the species is gone.
Vulnerable requires evidence of a qualifying threat.

questions.q: The cheetah vanished from India, officially declared extinct there in 1952, yet still survives in other countries. For India, the cheetah's status is best called
questions.explain: A species lost from one region but alive elsewhere is locally extinct or extirpated.
why_wrong: The species survives elsewhere.
Wild populations exist elsewhere.
It is not found only in India.

questions.q: A reserve allows villagers to graze cattle and collect fuelwood in limited areas while wildlife is protected. Which kind of protected area is this?
options: The core zone of a biosphere reserve
questions.explain: Sanctuaries permit certain human activities, whereas national parks prohibit grazing and forestry.
why_wrong: National parks prohibit grazing and forestry.
Core zones are strictly protected.
A botanical garden is an ex-situ facility.

questions.q: In a biosphere reserve, the legally protected zone where only research and monitoring are allowed, with no human disturbance, is the
questions.explain: The core zone is strictly protected and undisturbed.
why_wrong: The buffer zone allows limited research, education and tourism.
The outer transition zone includes settlements and sustainable activity.
This is an outer area where managed activities occur.

questions.q: Villagers in the Western Ghats protect a grove dedicated to a local deity, forbidding tree felling and hunting inside it. This is an example of
options: Seed banking in a cold vault
questions.explain: Sacred groves conserve species in their natural habitat, which is in-situ conservation.
why_wrong: Species remain in their natural habitat.
No animals are bred in captivity.
No seeds are being stored.

questions.q: A wildlife photographer wants to see the Indian one-horned rhinoceros in its natural habitat. Which protected area should she visit?
questions.explain: Kaziranga in Assam is famous for the one-horned rhinoceros.
why_wrong: Gir is known for the Asiatic lion.
Keoladeo is known for waterbirds.
Ranthambore is known for tigers.

questions.q: Which advantage belongs uniquely to in-situ conservation as opposed to ex-situ?
options: Species keep evolving in their natural ecosystem
Individuals can be protected from all disease
Population numbers can be controlled in closed enclosures
Seeds can be stored for decades
questions.explain: Natural habitats preserve ecological interactions and evolutionary processes.
why_wrong: No approach offers complete protection.
This is a feature of ex-situ management.
This is a feature of ex-situ gene banks.

questions.q: How does a biosphere reserve differ from a national park?
options: It has zones including settlements and sustainable use
It prohibits all human presence in every zone
It is created only in marine areas and oceans
It is an ex-situ facility like a zoo or garden
questions.explain: Biosphere reserves have core, buffer and transition zones, with people in the transition zone.
why_wrong: This describes the core zone only.
Biosphere reserves exist on land and coast.
It protects ecosystems in situ.

questions.q: Community reserves under India's wildlife law are best described as areas
options: Where community or private land is protected willingly
Declared only on government forest land without consent
Where all human use is banned
questions.explain: Community reserves are created on community or private land with local consent.
why_wrong: They need local willingness.
They permit community use.
Zoos are ex-situ.

questions.q: A botanist stores seeds of endangered wild rice relatives in a low-temperature vault at a national gene bank. This is
questions.explain: Conserving species outside their natural habitat, such as in seed banks, is ex-situ conservation.
why_wrong: The seeds are away from their natural habitat.
No habitat is being restored.
No tourism is involved.

questions.q: Sperm and eggs of an endangered animal are frozen in liquid nitrogen at about minus 196 degrees Celsius for future breeding. This technique is
questions.explain: Cryopreservation stores gametes or tissue at ultra-low temperatures.
why_wrong: This is toxin accumulation.
Micropropagation is tissue culture growth of plants.
This is pollution clean-up.

questions.q: Gharial hatchlings are raised in a captive centre and later released into the Chambal river. This combines
questions.explain: Animals bred in captivity and released into the wild is reintroduction.
why_wrong: This is illegal killing.
This protects in-situ habitat.
This is a threat, not a method.

questions.q: The last forest of a critically endangered species is destroyed by mining, leaving only a dozen animals. The most appropriate immediate action is
options: Leave them in place and wait
Capture them for ex-situ captive breeding
Declare the area a national park
questions.explain: With habitat gone, ex-situ breeding is the remaining way to keep the species.
why_wrong: They would die without habitat.
The habitat is already destroyed.
This would worsen the situation.

questions.q: Zoos that breed endangered animals face a genetic problem in the long run. Which is a genuine limitation of captive populations?
options: Captive animals gain unlimited genetic diversity over time
Captivity removes every disease risk from the animals
Captive breeding preserves natural ecological roles
Small founder groups lose variation and adapt poorly to the wild
questions.explain: Small captive groups face inbreeding and genetic drift, and captive adaptation can reduce survival after release.
why_wrong: Diversity tends to decline.
Disease can still occur.
The ecological role happens only in the wild.

questions.q: Why can seed banks NOT conserve all plant species, such as many tropical trees like jackfruit?
options: Recalcitrant seeds lose viability when dried or frozen
Their seeds are too large to be catalogued properly
They never produce any viable seeds
Seed banks only hold animal tissue samples
questions.explain: Recalcitrant seeds cannot tolerate drying or freezing, so conventional seed banking fails.
why_wrong: Size is not the issue.
Jackfruit produces seeds.
Seed banks hold seeds.

questions.q: A researcher studying the snow leopard, Tibetan wolf and chiru in the cold arid highlands of Ladakh is working in which Indian biogeographic zone?
questions.explain: The cold, arid region north of the main Himalaya is the Trans-Himalayan zone.
why_wrong: The Desert zone is the hot Thar region.
The Gangetic Plain is a fertile lowland.
The Coasts zone is the shoreline.

questions.q: A team monitoring the Great Indian Bustard among dune scrub and sparse grassland in Rajasthan is working in which biogeographic zone?
questions.explain: The Thar region of Rajasthan lies in the Desert zone.
why_wrong: The Western Ghats zone is a humid forest range.
The Islands zone is Andaman and Lakshadweep.
The North-East is a humid hill region.

questions.q: A primatologist studying hoolock gibbons in the humid forests of Assam and neighbouring states works in which zone?
questions.explain: The hoolock gibbon lives in the humid forests of north-eastern India.
why_wrong: The Semi-Arid zone is dry.
The Trans-Himalaya is cold and arid.
The Deccan holds dry and moist deciduous forests, not hoolock gibbons.

questions.q: A student studies the Nilgiri tahr and lion-tailed macaque, both limited to the humid forests along India's west. Which zone applies?
questions.explain: These species are endemic to the Western Ghats zone.
why_wrong: The Desert zone is arid.
The Gangetic Plain is a lowland plain.
The Trans-Himalaya is cold and arid.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ten biogeographic zones of India recognised by Rodgers and Panwar?
questions.explain: Sundaland is a hot spot, not an Indian biogeographic zone.
why_wrong: This is one of the ten zones.
This is one of the ten zones.
This is one of the ten zones.

questions.q: Which is the largest of India's biogeographic zones by area?
questions.explain: The Deccan Peninsula is the largest zone, covering a large part of peninsular India.
why_wrong: It is a cold high-altitude zone and not the largest.
The Islands zone is the smallest in area.
This is a narrow strip along the coast.

questions.q: Rodgers and Panwar's classification subdivides India's biogeographic zones into how many biotic provinces?
questions.explain: The classification recognises 10 zones, further subdivided into 25 biotic provinces.
why_wrong: Ten is the number of zones.
This is the global number of hot spots.
The classification has many more provinces.

questions.q: India has only about 2.4 percent of the world's land area yet holds a disproportionately large share of recorded species. Which best explains this?
options: Varied climates and topography, from peaks to islands
A uniform climate across the whole subcontinent
Absence of human settlement across the country
Having no forests or wetlands at all
questions.explain: Wide ranges of altitude, climate and habitat produce many ecological niches.
why_wrong: India's climate is highly varied.
India is densely populated.
India has varied forests.

questions.q: Which crop has its centre of origin and diversity in the Indian region?
questions.explain: Brinjal is among crops originating in the Indian region.
why_wrong: The potato originates in the Andes.
Maize originates in Mesoamerica.
The tomato originates in South America.

questions.q: A company wishes to obtain a medicinal plant from an Indian forest for commercial use. Which body's approval is required under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002?
questions.explain: The NBA regulates access to biological resources and ensures benefit sharing.
why_wrong: It regulates currency and banking.
It conducts elections.
It maps territory.

questions.q: Which feature is among the criteria for a country to be regarded as megadiversity?
questions.explain: Megadiversity countries have high species richness and high endemism.
why_wrong: Coastline is not a criterion.
Population is not a criterion.
Many megadiversity countries contain hot spots.

questions.q: Which historical factor contributed to the mixing of biota in the Indian region?
options: Isolation from all other land masses for millions of years
A single uniform climate throughout the region
The complete absence of mountain ranges
Northward drift of the Indian plate and collision with Eurasia
questions.explain: The drift and collision allowed Gondwanan and Eurasian elements to mix.
why_wrong: The collision with Eurasia ended isolation.
India's climates vary.
India has the Himalaya.

questions.q: Which statement about India's share of world biodiversity is accurate?
options: India has about 25 percent of the world's land area
India has 2.4 percent of world land but 7 to 8 percent of species
India holds under 1 percent of the world's recorded species
India has no endemic species at all, only widespread ones
questions.explain: India is a megadiversity country, with a high share of species relative to its area.
why_wrong: India has far less.
India holds much more.
India has many endemics.
